content: 1. The Feedback and Audit Implementation Guide Toolkit includes a Provider Survey Interpretation Guide and a Provider Survey of Family Planning Practices. The survey is divided into several parts: Part I focuses on demographics, Part II addresses contraceptive method availability, and Part III examines provider practices. 2. Questions 1-4 in the demographics section are purely informational. For questions 5-6, if a significant number of providers have not been trained on a specific contraceptive method, it may be beneficial to initiate formal training programs. 3. If contraceptive methods are unavailable or limited across the clinic, clinic management should investigate the reasons for this. If providers believe methods are unavailable but they are actually accessible, it is important to inform providers about what is available at the clinic and what requires referrals. 4. The response to question 8 can be used to evaluate access to intrauterine devices (IUDs) for nulliparous women. According to the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), IUDs are safe for use in women regardless of their parity. If providers rarely or never offer IUDs to nulliparous women, further investigation is needed to understand the reasons, and tailored interventions can be implemented to improve access. If providers are limiting use due to incorrect beliefs, targeted training on the safety and efficacy of IUDs in nulliparous women should be provided. If patient barriers exist, educational outreach may be necessary. If clinic protocols restrict access, they should be updated and disseminated accordingly. 5. If more tests are required than those indicated in the survey, it may be helpful to review the guidance in the Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR) regarding medically necessary exams and tests prior to initiating a contraceptive method. Unnecessary exams and tests can create barriers to accessing contraception. It is important to clarify what is required versus what is optional or available. Clinical protocols can help reduce unnecessary testing. 6. Responses to questions 10-13 can be used to assess access to contraceptive methods for adolescents and adult women. According to the SPR, all contraceptive methods should be available for initiation on the same day of the visit, regardless of menstrual timing, as long as the clinician is reasonably certain the client is not pregnant. If providers are not offering same-day services, additional training and education may be necessary. Clinical protocols for Quick Starting contraception can facilitate this process. 7. Routine pregnancy tests are not always required before initiating a contraceptive method. The SPR provides a clear checklist to help determine whether a pregnancy test is necessary. 8. All the time periods listed in question 15 are appropriate for starting contraception. This question emphasizes the importance of Quick Start protocols. The SPR offers guidance on when a contraceptive method can be safely initiated. 9. Question 16 helps identify barriers to providing contraception. If respondents frequently report barriers, the reasons they select (a-f) should be explored to identify interventions to improve access. For example: If (a) is selected, this may indicate supply chain issues. If (b) is selected, it may reflect a belief that most clients have complicated medical conditions, which is rarely the case. Reviewing the MEC with providers can ensure methods are not unnecessarily restricted due to medical conditions. If (c) is selected, it may indicate a need to address the safety of Quick Start protocols. If (d) is selected, while this may be justified in rare cases, it is not common for most clients. Reviewing the SPR checklist can help providers determine how to be reasonably certain a woman is not pregnant. If (e) is selected, reviewing SPR guidance on necessary exams and tests may be helpful. Only truly required tests should limit access to contraception. If (f) is selected, further provider training on method use or insertion may be necessary. 10. If providers are not comfortable with contraceptive counseling, additional training on counseling techniques may be beneficial. For clinics facing time or resource constraints, dividing counseling responsibilities among healthcare providers, health educators, or community health workers may be a practical solution. Each team member can cover specific topics to the extent they are comfortable.
